🐪 Good Wednesday afternoon. Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 598 words, a 2½-min. read. Thanks to Sheryl Miller for copy editing.

⚡️ Scoop: President Trump will attend a "New Golden Age Summit" in Washington tomorrow to hail the U.S. as a leader in "super intelligence," science and space. The administration says the summit "will bring together leading scientists and innovators to examine these changes and catalyze whole-of-nation efforts," Axios' Maria Curi and Alex Isenstadt report.
 
 
1 big thing — Report: ChatGPT for Teens poses "unacceptable risk"
 
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios

Common Sense Media says OpenAI's new ChatGPT for Teens poses an "unacceptable risk," Axios' Ina Fried reports.

  • That's after the nonprofit, which rates and recommends family media, found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users.

🧑‍💻 The group's Youth AI Safety Institute tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds.

  • It found that ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders, or sexual or romantic role-play — but says it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help.
  • ChatGPT missed more than 1 in 4 instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted, the group says.

The group also says that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert.

  • And it found that "study mode" — meant to help students work through problems rather than deliver immediate answers — could be circumvented.

🤔 The other side: OpenAI says it has issues with Common Sense Media's methodology and findings.

  • A spokesperson tells Axios: "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice."

2. 🤖 FCC may allow more robocalls
 
Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios

The FCC is considering a conservative group's request to loosen rules on political robocalls before November's midterm elections, including those with AI-generated voices.

🚫 Federal law currently bans most robocalls to cellphones unless the caller gets consent beforehand.

  • The petition calls for a waiver that would allow political groups to use artificial or prerecorded voices in unsolicited wireless calls.

⚠️ Consumer advocacy groups warn that the proposed change could trigger a surge of unwanted, partisan and potentially misleading calls in the critical final days of the elections.

  • The Republican-led FCC could rule on the proposal as soon as later this month.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
Graphic: NOAA
  1. 🌀 Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season's first Atlantic hurricane overnight, with impacts across the Gulf Coast and up into the interior Southeast. It would be the latest-forming Atlantic hurricane in the modern era. Latest forecast ... More from Axios' Carlie Kollath Wells.
  2. 💊 Scientists Henri B. Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that's been used to develop countless drugs. Go deeper.
  3. ⛳️ Spanish golf star Jon Rahm is exiting LIV Golf after deeming the league's reinvention plan "unacceptable." His departure marks a significant blow to the effort to create "LIV 2.0" after the league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. More from Nathan Bomey.
 
 
4. 🚛 1 for the road: Move to Detroit, get $15K
 
Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios

A new Detroit nonprofit is giving money to people who move to or pledge to stay in the Motor City, Axios Detroit's Annalise Frank reports.

💰 The first 13 winners of Move Detroit's "Make Detroit Home" grants are getting $15,000 each.

  • It's the first stage of the program, supported by billionaire and Rocket Mortgage co-founder Dan Gilbert.

CEO Hilary Doe said at a press conference: "This program is data-backed and focuses resources on our city's greatest asset: our people."
